doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Telling his father he will be a working musician
summary: Rowe asks about teaching; his father presses him on his plans and supports his choice of a music career.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: It was after graduation. Right after graduation almost. A few months.
Did you have — when you graduated, most of us at the time, with a few exceptions, everybody was going to go out and find teaching jobs.
But that wasn’t your intention was it?
No. What happened is that my father, who wanted me to do this, called me into the dining room, sat me down, and said okay what are you going to do with your life?

One of them questions. Because here my mother and my father said oh good he has a teaching degree he’ll have something to fall back on, that kind of — and a few times before that he called me in and I really didn’t know. I said I’m not quite sure yet. Finally this last time he called me in and I said, “I want to be a working musician, and I know how hard it’s going to be, I know it’s going to be tough, but that’s what I want to do. I’m ready to deal with it.” Little did I know — you know what I’m saying — that all your worries were true. But the thing is is that when I said that, because my father was the kind of person that, he may not agree with your decision but if you were sincere and convinced and determined to do something that he knew was at least going to try to bring some value he would support it. Because what happened is that of course in the time that we were graduating from Fredonia was in the middle of the Vietnam war. And they had a lottery system.
